text:
Rivers are the arteries of a landscape. They begin as trickles in high places, where snowmelt and rain gather in folds of rock, and they grow by collecting every stream and spring along their path. By the time a river reaches the sea, it carries water that has traveled through mountains, forests, farms, and cities, and it carries the sediment of all of them too.

A river never holds still. It cuts canyons over millions of years, then abandons a channel in a single flood. It builds deltas from the silt it drops when it slows, creating new land at the coast. Meanders wander across floodplains, pinching off into oxbow lakes and leaving behind rich soil that has fed civilizations from Egypt to China.

People have always settled beside rivers. They provide drinking water, irrigation, transport, fish, and power. Nearly every great city sits on a riverbank for these reasons. Yet the same rivers that sustain settlements also threaten them, rising without warning and sweeping away what was built too close.

Today rivers face dams, pollution, and the withdrawals of thirsty populations. Some no longer reach the ocean. Protecting them means recognizing that a river is not a resource alone but a living system, one that connects every place it touches.
